description: Checks whether a candidate can recognise signs of abuse, respond correctly to a disclosure, report and record concerns, keep safe boundaries and protect confidentiality.

competencies.name: Recognising Signs of Abuse
competencies.description: Knows the main forms of abuse and the warning signs in children

competencies.name: Responding to Disclosures
competencies.description: Responds calmly and correctly when a child tells about abuse

competencies.name: Reporting and Recording
competencies.description: Reports concerns to the right person and records facts accurately

competencies.name: Safe Behaviour and Boundaries
competencies.description: Follows safe codes of conduct and spots unsafe adult behaviour

competencies.name: Safe Recruitment and Confidentiality
competencies.description: Understands safe hiring checks and need-to-know confidentiality

questions.text: Which of these is a possible warning sign that a child is being abused?

options.text: Being late to school once because of heavy rain
Asking many questions during a science lesson
A sudden change in behaviour, such as fear of going home
Losing a pencil case and feeling sad about it

questions.explanation: Sudden, unexplained changes in behaviour, mood or attendance are common warning signs. One sign is not proof, but it should be taken seriously.

questions.text: Which of the following are recognised forms of child abuse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Physical abuse, such as hitting or burning a child
Setting age-appropriate homework for the class
Neglect, such as repeatedly failing to give food or care
Praising a pupil in front of the class
Emotional abuse, such as constant insults or threats

questions.explanation: Physical abuse, neglect and emotional abuse (as well as sexual abuse) are the main forms of child abuse. Homework and praise are normal school practice.

questions.text: A 10-year-old girl tells you privately that an adult relative touches her in ways that scare her. She begs, "Please do not tell anyone." What should you do?

options.text: Promise to keep it secret so that she continues to trust you and tells you more
Listen calmly, say you cannot keep this secret, and tell her you will get help
Visit the relative at his home and ask him to explain his side of the story first
Ask her many detailed questions until you are completely sure that it is true

questions.explanation: Never promise secrecy. Listen, reassure the child, explain that you must tell the person who can help, and do not investigate yourself.

questions.text: A child has just told you about abuse. Which response is most helpful?

options.text: "Are you sure? That sounds very unlikely, so think carefully."
"Why did you wait so long to tell anyone about this?"
"Do not tell anyone else; I will handle it myself quietly."
"Thank you for telling me. This is not your fault."

questions.explanation: The child needs to feel believed and not blamed. Questioning, blaming or promising to handle it alone can silence the child and delay protection.

questions.text: In most schools, who should a staff member first report a child protection concern to?

options.text: The school's designated safeguarding or child protection person
The parents of the child, before anyone else is told
The person suspected, so that he or she can respond
Other teachers in the staffroom, for their advice

questions.explanation: Concerns go to the designated safeguarding person (or head teacher where none is named). Telling the suspected person or discussing widely can put the child at risk.

questions.text: You suspect that the head teacher is abusing a pupil. Normally concerns go to the head teacher. What is the best action?

options.text: Say nothing, because the head teacher has full authority over all school matters
Question several pupils yourself first so that you can collect strong proof
Report to the school board or owner, or to the social welfare office or police
Wait until the end of term to see whether the pupil says more

questions.explanation: When the usual reporting person is involved, report to the next level up or to the external child protection authorities. Do not investigate yourself or delay.

questions.text: How should you record what a child tells you about abuse?

options.text: Write the child's own words with the date and time, as facts only
Write your opinion about whether the child is telling the truth
Write a short note from memory a few weeks later
Write nothing, so that the matter stays private

questions.explanation: Records should be prompt, factual and use the child's own words. Opinions and late notes weaken the record.

questions.text: A teacher gives extra lessons to one pupil after school. Which arrangement is safest?

options.text: In a closed office with the door shut so other pupils do not disturb them
At the teacher's house, where it is quiet and nobody will interrupt
In a visible place, or with another adult nearby and the door open
In a parked car while waiting for the pupil's parent to arrive

questions.explanation: Safe practice avoids being alone with a child out of sight. Open, visible settings protect both the child and the teacher.

questions.text: You notice that a colleague often gives one pupil gifts, phones the pupil at night, and drives the pupil home alone. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Write down factually what you have seen and when
Wait until you have clear proof before telling anyone
Warn the colleague privately and keep the matter quiet
Report your concern to the designated safeguarding person
Ask the pupil's classmates to find out what is happening

questions.explanation: These are warning signs of grooming. You should record facts and report promptly, and leave any investigation to the proper authorities.

questions.text: Which step is part of safe recruitment of staff who will work with children?

options.text: Hiring a friend of the head teacher without an interview or reference check
Checking identity, certificates and references, including work with children
Skipping checks for volunteers because they are not paid or only come briefly
Relying only on how confident the candidate looks

questions.explanation: Safe recruitment means verifying identity, qualifications and references for every person, paid or unpaid, who will have access to children.

questions.text: In the staffroom a colleague asks about a rumour that a pupil was abused. You know the details because you attended the case meeting. What is the best response?

options.text: Share a little so that the rumour stops spreading
Tell everyone in the staffroom so that all staff can watch the pupil closely
Politely decline, saying details go only to those who need to know
Post the main facts on the staff WhatsApp group so everyone is informed

questions.explanation: Child protection information is confidential and shared only with those who need it to protect the child. Gossip can harm the child and the investigation.

questions.text: A Standard 5 pupil, once cheerful, now sleeps in class, looks hungry, wears dirty clothes, and no adult attends meetings. What is the best first step?

options.text: Punish the pupil for sleeping so that it stops
Do nothing, since poverty and tiredness are not a child protection matter
Visit the home alone and confront the parents about how they treat the child
Record what you see and tell the designated safeguarding person

questions.explanation: These may be signs of neglect. Teachers should record observations and pass them to the designated person so the family's needs and the child's safety can be assessed.

description: Checks basic first aid knowledge for common school emergencies, hygiene and infection control, knowing when to refer, and keeping incident records.

competencies.name: Emergency Response and Priorities
competencies.description: Makes the scene safe, calls for help and acts in the right order

competencies.name: Bleeding, Burns and Injuries
competencies.description: Treats bleeding, burns, nosebleeds and suspected fractures correctly

competencies.name: Choking, Breathing and Seizures
competencies.description: Responds correctly to choking, seizures and a child who is not breathing

competencies.name: Illness and Infection Control
competencies.description: Uses good hygiene and handles common illnesses such as fever sensibly

competencies.name: Referral and Record Keeping
competencies.description: Knows when to refer to a health facility and records incidents properly

questions.text: You arrive at the scene of an accident at school. What should you do first?

options.text: Move the injured pupil immediately
Give the pupil something to drink
Start bandaging the most visible injury
Check that the area is safe for you and the pupil

questions.explanation: Check for danger first. If you become a casualty yourself, you cannot help anyone.

questions.text: A pupil has a nosebleed. What is the correct way to help?

options.text: Sit forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for about 10 minutes
Lay the pupil flat on the back and tilt the head back so the blood stops running
Push tissue paper deep into the nostril
Ask the pupil to keep blowing the nose hard to clear out the blood

questions.explanation: Leaning forward stops blood running down the throat, and firm pressure on the soft part of the nose usually stops the bleeding.

questions.text: A pupil cuts her leg deeply on a metal sheet and blood is flowing heavily. What is the best immediate action?

options.text: Wash the wound with soap and water for 10 minutes before doing anything else
Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth and keep pressing until help comes
Tie a tight string or wire above the wound and leave it there until the doctor comes
Leave the wound open so that it can clot by itself

questions.explanation: Direct pressure with a clean cloth is the first treatment for heavy bleeding. Keep pressing, and add more cloth rather than removing a soaked one.

questions.text: A pupil is scalded by hot porridge on the arm. What is the best first aid?

options.text: Cool the burn under running cool water for at least 10 minutes
Rub butter or cooking oil on the burn to seal it and keep the air out
Burst any blisters to let the fluid out and help the skin heal
Cover it with toothpaste to cool it and stop the pain

questions.explanation: Cooling with running water reduces damage and pain. Butter, oil and toothpaste can trap heat and cause infection, and blisters should be left intact.

questions.text: A child is choking and cannot cough, speak or breathe. What should you do?

options.text: Give water so the food is washed down, then ask the child to lie flat
Hold the child upside down by the ankles and shake until it drops out
Give 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, and call for help
Wait and watch to see whether it clears on its own before doing anything

questions.explanation: For severe choking, alternate back blows and abdominal thrusts for a child, and get help. Drinks and waiting do not clear a blocked airway.

questions.text: A pupil has a convulsive seizure in class. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Move hard objects away and cushion the head
Hold the pupil down firmly to stop the movements
Put a spoon or stick in the mouth to protect the tongue
Note the time, and place the pupil in the recovery position when the jerking stops
Get an adult to stay with the pupil and check breathing until fully awake

questions.explanation: Protect the head, never restrain or put anything in the mouth, time the seizure, and keep checking breathing afterwards. Call emergency help if it lasts too long or repeats.

questions.text: A pupil collapses on the field, does not respond and is not breathing normally. What is the best action?

options.text: Carry the pupil to the staff room, lay him on a bench, and wait quietly for him to wake up
Splash water on the face and wait a few minutes to see whether he wakes up
Give a sweet drink to restore energy
Shout for help, call emergency services, and start chest compressions if trained

questions.explanation: A person who is unresponsive and not breathing normally needs urgent help and CPR. Delay or moving the person wastes vital time.

questions.text: When should a first aider wash their hands?

options.text: Before and after treating a pupil, using soap and clean water
Only at the end of the day
Only if the hands look very dirty
Only after treating a pupil with blood on the skin

questions.explanation: Handwashing with soap before and after treatment protects both the helper and the pupil from infection.

questions.text: A pupil has a high fever, chills, headache and has vomited, in an area where malaria is common. What is the best action?

options.text: Send the pupil back to class after a cold drink and a short rest outside in the shade
Give leftover antibiotics from the staff room cupboard and watch the pupil
Keep the pupil resting, inform the parents, and refer to a clinic for testing
Wait until the next day to see if the fever goes away by itself, and only then decide

questions.explanation: Fever in a child may be malaria and needs prompt testing and treatment. Do not give unprescribed medicine or delay.

questions.text: Which details should be written in a school incident or first aid record?

options.text: Only the name of the pupil
Date, time, what happened, treatment given, and who was informed
Your opinion about who is to blame
A photo of the pupil to share on the class group

questions.explanation: A good record is factual: when and what happened, the care given and who was told. Opinions and photos shared on groups break confidentiality.

questions.text: During football a pupil hits his head. An hour later he vomits and seems very sleepy. What should you do?

options.text: Let him rest in class and check again tomorrow
Give him tea and send him back to the field
Arrange urgent medical care and inform his parents
Tell him to sleep at the sick bay and not disturb him

questions.explanation: Vomiting and drowsiness after a head injury can mean serious injury to the head. The pupil needs urgent medical assessment, and parents must be told.

questions.text: A pupil falls from a tree and cannot move his arm, which looks bent and is painful. What is the best first aid?

options.text: Pull the arm straight to see whether it moves normally and how much it hurts
Rub oil on the arm and massage it gently to ease the pain
Ask him to move the arm to test it
Keep the arm still and supported as found, then take him for medical care

questions.explanation: A suspected fracture should be supported and kept still, not straightened or moved, and the pupil taken to a health facility.

description: Checks a school transport driver's knowledge of vehicle checks, safe driving, child loading and supervision, emergency response and record keeping.

competencies.name: Pre-trip Vehicle Checks
competencies.description: Carries out and reports daily vehicle checks before carrying children

competencies.name: Safe Driving and Road Rules
competencies.description: Drives safely and lawfully with children on board

competencies.name: Loading, Offloading and Child Supervision
competencies.description: Loads, counts and offloads children safely and never overloads

competencies.name: Emergencies and Breakdowns
competencies.description: Responds correctly to breakdowns and accidents

competencies.name: Records and Compliance
competencies.description: Keeps logs and holds valid documents

questions.text: When should the daily vehicle check be done?

options.text: Once a week, on Monday morning
Only when a warning light comes on
After the last trip of the day
Every day before the first trip, before children board

questions.explanation: A walk-round check every day before loading finds faults while the vehicle is still safe to stop and repair.

questions.text: Which is a safe driver practice when children are on board?

options.text: Answering phone calls while driving, if the road ahead looks clear and empty
Keeping the phone away and not using it while the vehicle is moving
Driving fast on empty stretches of road to save time on the route
Allowing children to stand in the aisle if the bus is full

questions.explanation: Phone use distracts the driver. Children must be seated, and speed must suit the road, not the clock.

questions.text: Which items should be checked before the school run? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tyre condition and pressure
Brakes and brake pedal feel
Whether the radio and music system works
Whether the outside of the vehicle has been washed
Lights, indicators and mirrors

questions.explanation: Tyres, brakes, lights, indicators and mirrors are safety-critical. Music and cleanliness do not affect safe operation.

questions.text: At a stop, a child drops a book near the rear wheel just as you are about to move. What is the best action?

options.text: Reverse slowly towards the child so that the child can step out and pick up the book
Stop, apply the handbrake, check around, and fetch the book or ask the attendant
Drive off and tell the child to leave it on the road because the bus is already late
Let the child run back to pick it up quickly while the engine keeps running

questions.explanation: Never move until you know exactly where every child is. A child near a wheel can be hidden from the mirrors.

questions.text: After offloading at the last stop, what should the driver do before leaving the vehicle?

options.text: Lock the doors immediately to prevent theft
Look only in the rear mirror
Walk through the vehicle and check every seat for a sleeping or hiding child
Ask the last child to confirm nobody is left

questions.explanation: A full walk-through at the end of the route prevents a child being left behind, for example asleep on a back seat.

questions.text: You are 20 minutes late for pick-up and parents are waiting. The road ahead is clear. What should you do?

options.text: Drive faster than the safe speed to catch up with the time lost on the route
Skip the last two stops on the route to save time and avoid more delay
Drive through the junctions without slowing down so as to make up time
Keep to safe speeds and road rules and phone the school about the delay

questions.explanation: Being late is never a reason to take risks with children. Inform the school and arrive safely.

questions.text: A manager asks you to carry 15 extra children standing in the aisle "just this once". What should you do?

options.text: Agree, but drive more slowly than usual and keep to the quietest roads
Agree if the children hold the seat rails tightly and the extra ones sit in the aisle
Refuse to exceed the seats, and ask for a second trip or another vehicle
Agree, but only for the shorter route and only on the first morning trip

questions.explanation: Overloading and standing children greatly increase injury risk in a crash or sudden stop. Each child needs a seat.

questions.text: Your vehicle breaks down on a narrow road with children on board. What is the best action?

options.text: Park in the middle of the road so that other drivers can see you from far away
Ask the older children to get out and push the bus off the road
Keep driving slowly on the flat tyre to the next town while the children stay seated
Move off the road, switch on hazards, set the triangle, and keep the children safe

questions.explanation: Make the vehicle visible, keep children away from traffic, and call for help. Do not let children stay in dangerous positions.

questions.text: After a minor collision, a child says her neck hurts. What should you do?

options.text: Stop, switch off, avoid moving her unnecessarily, and call for medical help
Tell her to move her neck around to see whether it hurts, then decide what next
Carry her quickly to the front seat and drive on to the school as fast as you can
Say nothing and continue the trip to avoid delays, and report it the next day

questions.explanation: Neck pain after a collision may be a serious injury. Keep the child still unless in danger, and get emergency help.

questions.text: Which documents must a school driver keep valid and available?

options.text: A photo of the vehicle for the school website
The school's timetable for pupils
A list of the best routes drawn by the driver
A valid driving licence, vehicle insurance and required inspection documents

questions.explanation: A driver must be legally licensed and the vehicle insured and inspected as required. These protect children and the school.

questions.text: While driving, you notice the brake pedal feels soft. What is the best action?

options.text: Report it to your supervisor, and do not carry children until it is repaired
Continue the route and tell the mechanic at the end of the week when it is convenient
Pump the brakes harder on each stop and carry on with the usual route and timetable
Wait to see whether the problem gets worse before you tell anyone about the brakes

questions.explanation: A brake defect is a safety fault. It must be logged, reported and fixed before the vehicle carries children again.

questions.text: On which side of the road do vehicles drive in Tanzania?

options.text: The right side
The left side
Either side, depending on traffic
The side with fewer potholes

questions.explanation: Tanzania drives on the left side of the road.

description: Checks school kitchen staff knowledge of hygiene, preventing cross-contamination, temperature control and storage, menu planning and kitchen safety.

competencies.name: Personal Hygiene
competencies.description: Keeps good personal hygiene and stays away from food work when ill

competencies.name: Cross-Contamination and Safe Handling
competencies.description: Prevents bacteria spreading from raw to ready-to-eat food

competencies.name: Temperature Control and Storage
competencies.description: Cooks, cools, reheats and stores food at safe temperatures

competencies.name: Menu Planning and Portions
competencies.description: Plans balanced menus, controls portions and protects pupils with allergies

competencies.name: Kitchen Safety and Cleaning
competencies.description: Works safely in the kitchen and cleans correctly

questions.text: When must kitchen staff wash their hands with soap and water?

options.text: Only at the end of the working day, when the kitchen is closed and cleaned
Only when the hands look visibly dirty or sticky after working
After using the toilet and after handling raw meat or fish
Only after eating a meal or drinking tea during the break

questions.explanation: Hands carry germs that cannot be seen. Wash after the toilet, after raw meat, waste or eating, and before food preparation.

questions.text: A cook has diarrhoea and vomiting this morning but says he can work because the kitchen is short of staff. What is correct?

options.text: He may continue cooking if he wears gloves and a mask the whole time
He may work only on the cold dishes, away from the hot cooking area
He should stay off food handling until he is well and cleared
He may work if he washes his hands more often during the shift

questions.explanation: People with diarrhoea or vomiting can spread illness through food. They must stay away from food work until well and cleared.

questions.text: Why should raw meat and ready-to-eat food use separate boards and knives?

options.text: So that the knives stay sharp longer
So that bacteria from raw food do not pass to food that will not be cooked again
So that the food keeps its flavour
So that the boards can be washed less often

questions.explanation: Raw foods carry bacteria. Using separate equipment stops these spreading to food eaten without further cooking.

questions.text: You have just cut raw chicken and now must slice tomatoes for the salad. What should you do?

options.text: Wipe the knife and board with a dry cloth, then carry on slicing the tomatoes
Wash your hands, then use a clean board and knife, or wash and sanitise them
Rinse the board with cold water only and carry on with the same knife
Slice the tomatoes on the same board without cleaning it, since they will be washed later

questions.explanation: Salad is not cooked, so any chicken bacteria left on equipment will reach the pupils. Clean thoroughly or use separate equipment.

questions.text: What does the "danger zone" for food mean?

options.text: The range between about 5 degrees and 60 degrees Celsius, where bacteria multiply fastest
Temperatures above 100 degrees Celsius
Temperatures below freezing
Any food stored near the cooker

questions.explanation: Bacteria grow quickly between roughly 5 and 60 degrees Celsius. Food should be kept cold or served hot, and not left in this range.

questions.text: Rice and beans were cooked for lunch and some is left over. Which practices are safe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cool it quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate within about two hours
Leave the pot covered on the stove overnight
Reheat it until steaming hot all the way through
Mix the leftover into a fresh batch so it is not wasted
Throw away food that has stood at room temperature for many hours

questions.explanation: Leftovers must be cooled and chilled promptly and reheated until very hot. Food left too long in the danger zone should be thrown away.

questions.text: What does "first in, first out" (FIFO) mean in a food store?

options.text: Use the newest stock first
Use the cheapest stock first
Use the heaviest sacks first
Use the oldest stock first

questions.explanation: FIFO rotates stock so older items are used before they spoil or expire.

questions.text: Where should sacks of maize flour and beans be stored?

options.text: Directly on the floor, against the wall, to save space on the shelves
On racks off the floor, in a dry, ventilated, pest-proof store
In the open yard under a sheet, so that the store stays free
Next to the cleaning chemicals to save space in the small store room

questions.explanation: Dry foods need to be kept off the floor, dry and protected from pests and chemicals to avoid spoilage and contamination.

questions.text: You plan weekly meals for 300 boarders on a limited budget. Which menu approach is best?

options.text: The cheapest staple only, every day, to save money
Rice and meat every day, because pupils like it
Whatever the pupils ask for on each day
A staple with beans, fish or eggs, plus vegetables, with variety through the week

questions.explanation: A balanced school menu combines staple foods, protein, and vegetables or fruit, with variety, and can still be affordable.

questions.text: The parent of a pupil has told the school that the pupil is allergic to groundnuts, and today's sauce contains groundnuts. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the groundnuts from the pupil's plate only and serve it from the same pot
Tell the pupil to eat a small amount to see whether any reaction happens
Give the pupil the same food and watch carefully for any signs of a reaction
Prepare a separate safe meal with clean utensils and tell the serving staff

questions.explanation: Allergens can cause serious reactions even in small amounts. Prepare a separate safe meal and avoid cross-contact.

questions.text: Cooking oil in a pan catches fire. What should you do?

options.text: Pour a full bucket of water onto the burning pan to put the fire out quickly
Turn off the heat if safe, and cover the pan with a lid or damp cloth
Carry the pan outside quickly while the oil is still burning
Fan the flames to blow the fire out before it spreads further

questions.explanation: Water makes oil fires spread violently. Switch off the heat if safe and smother the flames by cutting off air.

questions.text: How should kitchen work surfaces be cleaned?

options.text: Wipe with a damp cloth only, then leave the surface to dry in the air
Spray with air freshener so that the surface smells clean and fresh
Clean with detergent and water first, then sanitise
Sweep with a dry broom and then leave it until the next day

questions.explanation: Cleaning removes dirt and grease, and sanitising then reduces germs. Sanitiser does not work well on dirty surfaces.

description: Checks knowledge of preventive maintenance, hazard control, fire safety, cleaning and sanitation, and managing contractors in a school setting.

competencies.name: Preventive Maintenance
competencies.description: Plans regular inspections and servicing before faults become failures

competencies.name: Hazard Identification and Control
competencies.description: Spots hazards and makes them safe quickly

competencies.name: Fire Safety
competencies.description: Knows fire basics, extinguishers, exits and evacuation

competencies.name: Cleaning and Sanitation
competencies.description: Keeps toilets, classrooms and water points clean and hygienic

competencies.name: Contractor and Repair Management
competencies.description: Hires, supervises and signs off contractor work properly

questions.text: Which is an example of preventive maintenance?

options.text: Replacing a generator only after it has broken down completely
Servicing the generator on a regular schedule
Repairing a roof only after it has started to leak badly
Ignoring small faults until they get worse and become big ones

questions.explanation: Preventive maintenance means regular servicing and inspection to prevent breakdowns, which is cheaper and safer than emergency repair.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of a maintenance schedule and log?

options.text: To plan tasks, assign who does them, and record what was done
To show visitors that the school is busy
To replace the need for inspections
To give the head teacher a list to read once a year

questions.explanation: A schedule and log make sure work is done on time and give a history of repairs and costs for future decisions.

questions.text: The rainy season is coming. Which tasks should the maintenance team do now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clear gutters and drains
Repaint the outside walls first
Inspect roof sheets and repair loose or damaged ones
Wait until leaks are reported before checking the roofs
Postpone drainage work until the rains end

questions.explanation: Clearing drainage and fixing roofs before the rains prevents flooding and leaks. Waiting for reports means damage has already happened.

questions.text: You see exposed electrical wires hanging in a corridor used by pupils. What is the best action?

options.text: Wrap the wires with insulating tape yourself and leave them where they are
Leave it until the monthly inspection
Keep people away with a barrier, report it, and call a qualified electrician
Tell pupils to avoid the area but put up no sign or barrier and report nothing

questions.explanation: Exposed live wires can kill. Make the area safe immediately and use a qualified person for the repair.

questions.text: A corridor has just been mopped and is wet. What should you do?

options.text: Put up a "wet floor" sign until it is dry
Tell pupils to run through quickly so that they do not slip on it
Leave the area with no warning and let people find their own way
Close the school until the floor dries, even if that takes the whole day

questions.explanation: A warning sign reduces slips and falls while the floor is wet.

questions.text: Which three things does a fire need to burn?

options.text: Heat, smoke and running water
Fuel, wind and cold water
Heat, fuel and oxygen
Oxygen, ash and heat from the sun

questions.explanation: Fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen. Removing any one of them puts the fire out.

questions.text: Which is suitable for fighting a fire in electrical equipment?

options.text: A bucket of water
A water extinguisher
A wet blanket thrown over the plugs
A CO2 or dry powder extinguisher

questions.explanation: Water conducts electricity and can cause shock. CO2 or dry powder extinguishers are designed for electrical fires.

questions.text: During a fire drill, a teacher counts the class at the assembly point and one pupil is missing. What should the teacher do?

options.text: Run back into the building to search alone
Tell the head teacher or fire team immediately and do not re-enter the building
Wait ten minutes to see if the pupil arrives
Send other pupils back to search the classroom

questions.explanation: Re-entering endangers more lives. Report the missing person at once so trained responders can search.

questions.text: You find an exit door padlocked during school hours "to prevent theft". What should you do?

options.text: Leave it as it is, because theft is the greater risk at night in this area
Lock the other exits as well so that nobody can get in from outside
Keep the only key with the watchman at the gate on the far side of the whole compound
Report it to management and have the lock removed so the door opens from inside

questions.explanation: Exits must be unlocked and clear whenever people are in the building, or people could be trapped in a fire.

questions.text: Before hiring a contractor for electrical work, what should you check?

options.text: That the contractor is a relative of a staff member who recommended him
That the contractor has the lowest price, whatever the quality of the work done
Licence or qualifications, references, and a written quotation with scope
That the contractor owns a new vehicle and has a smart business card

questions.explanation: Verify competence and agree a written scope and price. Poor electrical work is a serious safety risk.

questions.text: Which best keeps school toilets hygienic?

options.text: Cleaning only when the toilets smell
A cleaning schedule with a signed checklist, and soap and water at handwashing points
Cleaning once at the start of the term
Locking the toilets between lessons

questions.explanation: Regular, checked cleaning and working handwashing reduce disease spread among pupils.

questions.text: A contractor finishes repairing a classroom roof and asks for full payment immediately. What should you do before paying?

options.text: Pay now in full, to keep the contractor friendly and willing to return
Pay half now and forget the check, since the work looks fine from outside
Ask the pupils whether the roof looks good and pay if they are satisfied
Inspect the work against the written scope and quotation, then sign off

questions.explanation: Check that the work meets the agreed scope and quality before payment. This protects school funds and safety.

description: Checks safe storage and labelling of chemicals, laboratory safety practice, equipment and inventory care, practical preparation, and waste and emergency response.

competencies.name: Chemical Storage and Labelling
competencies.description: Stores and labels chemicals by hazard in a secure place

competencies.name: Laboratory Safety and PPE
competencies.description: Uses protective equipment and safe working methods

competencies.name: Equipment Care and Inventory
competencies.description: Looks after equipment and keeps stock records current

competencies.name: Practical Preparation
competencies.description: Prepares practicals in advance with enough safe materials

competencies.name: Waste Disposal and Emergencies
competencies.description: Disposes of waste safely and responds correctly to spills and accidents

questions.text: What is the best way to store chemicals in a school laboratory store?

options.text: In alphabetical order on one shelf, regardless of the hazards
In a locked, cool, ventilated store, grouped by hazard and clearly labelled
In the preparation room so teachers can reach them quickly
Wherever there is space, with the heaviest bottles on top

questions.explanation: Chemicals should be locked away and grouped by hazard so that incompatible ones, such as acids and bases, are kept apart.

questions.text: You find a bottle with a faded label. What is the correct action?

options.text: Smell it carefully to identify it before deciding what to do with it
Pour it down the sink to be safe and rinse the bottle for reuse
Use it in a class practical, since it is probably only water or a mild solution
Do not use it, mark it unknown, and seek advice on safe disposal

questions.explanation: Unidentified chemicals can be dangerous. Never use, smell or taste them. Isolate and ask a qualified person for safe disposal.

questions.text: Which information should be on a chemical container label? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chemical name and concentration
The name of the pupil who last used it
Hazard warning, such as corrosive or flammable
The price paid at purchase
Date received or prepared

questions.explanation: A label should identify the substance, warn of its hazard, and show when it was received or prepared.

questions.text: What is the minimum protective gear for a pupil doing a chemistry practical?

options.text: Normal clothes and open sandals, as long as the experiment looks simple
Gloves only, since goggles and aprons make pupils too hot
A lab coat, safety goggles, closed shoes, and tied-back hair
No protection if the chemicals are weak or the amounts are very small

questions.explanation: Eyes and skin must be protected from splashes, even with dilute solutions. Closed shoes and tied hair also prevent injuries.

questions.text: You see a pupil about to draw sodium hydroxide solution into a pipette by mouth. What should you do?

options.text: Let him continue if he is careful and does not swallow any of the liquid
Tell him to rinse his mouth afterwards and carry on with the practical
Ask him to hold his breath while doing it and spit out any liquid
Stop him at once and show him how to use a pipette filler

questions.explanation: Never pipette by mouth. Chemicals can be swallowed or inhaled, so use a pipette filler or bulb.

questions.text: How should you dilute concentrated acid?

options.text: Add the acid slowly to the water, stirring
Add the water quickly and all at once to the acid
Pour both together at the same time into a flask
Heat the acid first, then add water to it fast

questions.explanation: Always add acid to water slowly. Adding water to concentrated acid can cause violent boiling and splashing.

questions.text: Acid splashes onto a pupil's forearm. What is the right immediate action?

options.text: Wipe it off with a dry cloth
Put sodium hydroxide solution on it to neutralise the acid
Rinse under running water for at least 10 minutes, remove any wet clothing, and seek help
Cover it with butter

questions.explanation: Plenty of running water dilutes and removes the chemical. Do not use neutralising chemicals on skin, because that can cause further damage.

questions.text: After a practical, you have leftover solution containing lead or copper salts. What should you do?

options.text: Pour it onto the school garden so that the plants and soil absorb it
Pour it down the sink with plenty of water running to dilute it
Collect it in a labelled waste container for proper disposal
Leave it in an open beaker in the lab to evaporate over some days

questions.explanation: Heavy-metal waste is toxic and harms water and soil. It must be collected, labelled and disposed of safely.

questions.text: How should a microscope be cared for after use?

options.text: Remove the slide, clean lenses with lens paper, lower the stage, cover it
Leave the slide on the stage ready for the next class to use
Wipe the lenses with a cloth soaked in water, then dry them with the same cloth
Store it uncovered on the window sill where the light is good

questions.explanation: Cleaning with lens paper, removing slides and covering the microscope protect the lenses and the mechanism.

questions.text: A stock check shows several expired chemicals and fewer beakers than the register says. What is the best action?

options.text: Remove the expired chemicals from the register and say nothing
Ignore the beakers because glass often breaks
Update the register, set the expired items aside for safe disposal, and report the shortages
Use the expired chemicals first so they are not wasted

questions.explanation: Records must match what is in stock. Expired chemicals need safe disposal, and shortages must be reported and replaced.

questions.text: What should a laboratory technician do before a practical lesson?

options.text: Try the experiment, label materials for each group, and check safety items
Prepare materials only after pupils arrive, while they wait in the lab
Give each pupil as much chemical as they want so that nobody runs short or waits
Leave all preparation to the pupils while the teacher marks books

questions.explanation: Trying the practical in advance and preparing enough labelled material reduces accidents and wasted time.

questions.text: A planned practical releases a toxic gas. What should you do?

options.text: Let pupils do it at their desks with the windows closed to keep the smell inside
Use a fume cupboard or ventilated area, or a teacher demonstration with small amounts
Let each pupil use a larger amount to see the result more clearly
Skip the risk assessment, since the teacher has done this experiment many times before

questions.explanation: Toxic gases should be produced only in small quantities with strong ventilation, and often as a controlled teacher demonstration.
